items.title: L12: Presenting to a sceptical audience and handling challenge
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Communicating and Influencing (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Many senior-grade presentation exercises are staged so that the panel plays a sceptical audience: a director who thinks your recommendation is too expensive, or a stakeholder who dislikes the change. The panel is not being hostile for its own sake. It is checking how you influence people who disagree, which is central to the Communicating and Influencing Behaviour.

Several habits help. Listen to the whole question before answering, and if the challenge is unclear, check it back: 'Is your concern the cost in year one, or the total cost?' Acknowledge any valid point before you respond, because defending at once suggests you are not listening. Then answer with evidence rather than assertion: a figure, a comparison or a risk you have already considered. If the challenge exposes a real weakness in your proposal, accept it and say how you would deal with it. Panels respect candidates who adjust a position for good reason and are uneasy with those who never concede anything.

If you do not know, say so plainly and explain how you would find out, and by when. Guessing a figure or inventing a precedent is a much greater risk than a short admission. Do not become defensive, sarcastic or apologetic, and keep your tone and pace steady.

Keep control of your message. After answering a challenge, tie back to your central recommendation in a sentence, so that a series of questions does not pull the session off course. If a question is outside the brief, say what you can speak to and suggest who could answer the rest.

Finally, treat the challenge as part of the exercise rather than an interruption of it. Candidates who stay courteous and evidence-led under pressure usually score better than those who deliver the prepared talk flawlessly but struggle in questions.

questions.prompt: The panel, playing a sceptical director, says your recommendation is too expensive. What is the strongest first move?

options.text: Offer to reduce the scope straight away, so that the objection is removed before it takes hold of the discussion
Check which cost concern they mean, acknowledge it, then answer with a figure or comparison
Explain that cost decisions belong to finance colleagues and cannot sensibly be settled in this kind of exercise
Restate the benefits of the recommendation more forcefully, so that the cost looks smaller by comparison with them

questions.hint: Clarifying and acknowledging before answering shows listening and lets you respond to the real concern.

questions.prompt: A panellist's question exposes a genuine weakness in your proposal. What does the strongest candidate do?

options.text: Suggest that the panel is judging the proposal against criteria that you were never given in the brief
Say that the weakness is outside the brief and move on to the next question without discussing it
Accept the point and explain how the weakness would be managed
Defend the proposal as it stands, because conceding anything undermines the whole of your recommendation

questions.hint: Panels respect candidates who adjust for good reason and show how risks would be handled.

questions.prompt: You are asked for a figure you do not have. Which reply is best?

options.text: I would need the panel to tell me which assumptions to use before I could give any sensible answer
I believe it is around a million pounds, and I can confirm the exact number later if the panel needs it
That figure is not central to the recommendation, so I would leave it out of any version of the proposal
I do not have that figure to hand; I would get it from finance by Friday and send it on

questions.hint: Admitting a gap and saying how you will close it protects credibility and honesty.

questions.prompt: Why is it useful to check back an unclear challenge before answering it?

options.text: It buys you thinking time, so that your next answer can be longer and better prepared
It lets you steer the discussion on to a topic where your evidence is stronger
You answer the real concern, and it shows the panel you are listening
It signals to the panel that their question was badly phrased and needs rewording

questions.hint: Checking back prevents answering the wrong question.

questions.prompt: After four questions on cost, the session has drifted away from your central message. What should you do?

options.text: Offer to restart the presentation from the beginning, so that the central message is heard in full
Answer the latest question, then tie back to your main recommendation in a sentence
Ask the panel politely to move on to a different topic, so that you can return to your own structure
Hold your conclusion back until the session ends, so that it is the last thing the panel hears

questions.hint: A brief tie-back keeps control of the message without dismissing questions.

questions.prompt: Which response to a challenge is most likely to lose marks?

options.text: Becoming defensive and repeating the same point more loudly
Asking for the question to be rephrased before replying
Agreeing with a fair criticism and saying what would change
Pausing briefly before answering a difficult question

questions.hint: Defensiveness suggests poor listening and weak influencing.

questions.prompt: A question falls outside the brief, on a policy area you know little about. What is the best answer?

options.text: Offer an educated guess, so that the panel sees you are willing to engage with anything they raise
Say the question is out of scope and decline to comment, since the brief did not cover it
Link the question to a related topic you know well and answer that one instead
Say what you can speak to and suggest who could answer the rest

questions.hint: Honest boundaries with a pointer to the right person show judgement.

questions.prompt: Why does a panel play a sceptical audience in a presentation exercise?

options.text: To compare your performance with a model answer the panel holds
To assess how you influence people who disagree with you
To check that you can predict every possible objection in advance
To see whether you will drop your recommendation as soon as it is questioned

questions.hint: Influencing sceptics is central to senior roles.

questions.prompt: Which is the strongest way to answer a challenge with evidence?

options.text: Point out how much work has already gone into the proposal so far
Mention that senior colleagues backed the proposal when it was first discussed
Quote a general principle that the audience is likely to agree with already
Use a specific figure, a comparison or a risk you have already considered

questions.hint: Specific evidence persuades better than assertion or authority.

questions.prompt: A candidate answers every challenge with 'That is a very good question' and then repeats the prepared talk. What is the weakness?

options.text: They are not engaging with the actual point raised
They are praising the panel too much for it to sound sincere
They are showing nerves by speaking too quickly each time
They are using too many words in each of their answers

questions.hint: Answers must engage with the challenge, not recycle the script.

items.title: L12: Written exercises with competing priorities and incomplete data
items.source: Civil Service Jobs candidate guidance and Success Profiles (GOV.UK)
items.body:
At HEO and above, written exercises often combine a short deadline with material that is incomplete, out of date or contradictory. You may be asked for a submission recommending one of several options, a response to a letter, or a note for a senior official ahead of a meeting. The assessors are testing judgement as much as writing: what you choose to include, what you flag and what you decide not to claim.

Start by deciding the purpose and the reader. What decision should the reader take, and what do they need to know to take it? Write a one-line summary before you write anything else, and test every paragraph against it. A paragraph that does not help the reader decide can usually be cut.

Use the evidence honestly. When the pack gives out-of-date numbers, say so and say how it affects your advice. Where data is missing, set out the assumption you have made and the risk of being wrong, rather than presenting an estimate as a fact. Distinguish clearly between what is known, what is judged and what is uncertain. A good note might say: 'The latest figures are from 2019 and may understate demand; if demand has grown by a quarter, option B becomes more expensive than option A.'

Present options fairly. Give each a short statement of benefits, costs and risks, then recommend one and say why you rejected the others. Include next steps, an owner and a date where possible, and note anything that needs the approval of another person, such as finance or legal.

Keep the tone neutral and professional. Avoid emotive language and personal opinion unless asked for your view. A submission advises; it does not lobby. Proofread, check that your numbers add up and that your recommendation matches your reasoning.

questions.prompt: What should you do before writing a submission under time pressure?

options.text: List every fact from the pack in order, so that nothing is left out of the note
Write the background section first, so that the context is fully set out for the reader
Decide what decision the reader must take and write a one-line summary of your advice
Draft the options table first and leave the recommendation until the very end

questions.hint: A clear purpose and summary guide what goes in and what is cut.

questions.prompt: The pack's demand figures are several years old. How should you handle them?

options.text: Use them, say they may be out of date and show how this could affect the advice
Use them without comment, since the pack is the only evidence the exercise supplies
Leave them out altogether, because figures this old cannot be relied on for any purpose
Adjust them upwards by an amount you think is reasonable and present the result as fact

questions.hint: Honest handling of weak data shows judgement and integrity.

questions.prompt: Which sentence best separates what is known from what is judged?

options.text: Uptake is 40 per cent and will rise further, because uptake always rises over time
Uptake is unknown, so no recommendation can be made without a new survey
Uptake is probably quite high and is likely to be somewhere around 40 per cent
The 2019 survey found 40 per cent uptake; I judge it is likely to be higher now

questions.hint: Distinguishing evidence from judgement makes advice credible and honest.

questions.prompt: When presenting three options fairly, what should the note include for each?

options.text: A ranking of the options, with the reasons held back for discussion afterwards
A description of each option, with the recommended one set out in much more detail
Only the benefits of each option, to keep the note short and positive for the reader
A short statement of benefits, costs and risks, then why the others were rejected

questions.hint: Fair comparison supports the reader's own decision.

questions.prompt: Which element makes a recommendation most actionable?

options.text: A request that the reader replies with any comments
A longer discussion of the background to the issue
Next steps, with an owner and a date where possible
A list of other people who might be interested

questions.hint: Concrete next steps turn advice into action.

questions.prompt: A submission advises a senior official. Which tone is appropriate?

options.text: Cautious and non-committal, so that you cannot be shown to have been wrong
Persuasive and emphatic, to make sure the recommended option is the one chosen
Informal and friendly, so that you build a rapport with the reader from the start
Neutral and professional, setting out advice and reasons

questions.hint: A submission advises rather than lobbies.

questions.prompt: You find that your recommendation conflicts with a number you reported earlier in the note. What is the best action?

options.text: Add a footnote saying that the figures are indicative and may not agree with the text
Delete the earlier figure and keep the recommendation, because the advice is what matters
Leave it as it is, because the reader is unlikely to notice a difference of this kind
Correct the figure or the recommendation so that they agree, and flag any change the reader has already seen

questions.hint: Consistency between numbers and advice is essential, and honest correction protects trust.

questions.prompt: Your recommendation depends on legal clearance you do not have. How should the note handle it?

options.text: Leave legal issues out and let the reader raise them if they wish to
Say that the recommendation has legal approval, in anticipation that it will be given
Recommend a different option that avoids any legal question altogether
State clearly that it depends on legal clearance and say who needs to give it

questions.hint: Flagging dependencies keeps advice accurate and honest.

questions.prompt: Why should you cut a paragraph that does not help the reader decide?

options.text: It makes your note longer than other candidates' notes
It suggests that you have not read the whole of the pack
It dilutes the message and uses up the reader's time and attention
It may contain errors that an assessor is likely to find

questions.hint: Selection is part of the skill being assessed.

questions.prompt: Which closing line best suits a submission?

options.text: Option B is an interesting choice that could be considered alongside the others
I hope this is helpful and am happy to discuss any part of it further
Further analysis may be needed before a decision is reached on the way forward
I recommend option B, subject to legal clearance, with first steps agreed by 30 June

questions.hint: A clear recommendation, condition and date are what a submission should end on.

items.title: L12: Panel dynamics: interruptions, silent panellists and remote panels
items.source: Civil Service Commission Recruitment Principles and Civil Service Jobs guidance
items.body:
Panels vary in how they behave, and a candidate who understands the common patterns stays steadier. One panellist may ask most of the questions while another says very little. The quieter panellist is often watching, taking notes or preparing a later question, and is as important as the others when scoring. Treat them equally: give each some eye contact and thank each for their questions.

Some panellists interrupt. They may do so to keep to time, to move you from background to action, or to probe a point. If a panellist cuts in, stop, answer the point and then, if needed, return to your answer: 'Shall I go on to the result?' Do not take it as a sign of failure. Where one panellist is challenging and another friendly, respond to both with the same professionalism. The challenging manner is rarely personal and may be there to see how you respond under pressure.

In remote or hybrid interviews, panellists may join from different places and some may keep their camera off. Look at the camera when speaking, not at yourself, and pause slightly longer than usual between sentences to avoid talking over others. If audio fails, say so at once rather than guessing. If someone joins late, stay calm; the chair will normally recap.

When the panel includes someone from another department or a professional specialist, adapt your language: avoid your own department's acronyms and explain terms.

Note what a panel may not do. They should not ask about your age, marital status, health, religion or plans to have children. A panel member who asks should be politely redirected to the role's requirements, and you can raise it afterwards with the recruitment contact. Throughout, remember that panels are asked to apply the same criteria to every candidate.

questions.prompt: One panellist asks every question while another says nothing. How should you treat the silent panellist?

options.text: Ask the chair whether the silent panellist is listening to your answers
Focus on the questioner, because the silent panellist probably has little say in the outcome
Include them in your eye contact, as they will almost certainly be scoring too
Direct a question to the silent panellist, to draw them into the conversation

questions.hint: Every panellist usually scores, whether or not they speak.

questions.prompt: A panellist interrupts you midway through describing the Situation. What is the best response?

options.text: Carry on until you reach the end of the section, so that your answer keeps its structure
Speed up to cover the rest of your answer before you are cut off again
Ask them politely to wait until you have finished, because your answer is nearly complete
Stop, answer their point and offer to move on to the action and result

questions.hint: Interruptions often keep to time or push you to the action, and adapting shows listening.

questions.prompt: Why might a panellist adopt a challenging manner?

options.text: To test whether you will simply agree with anything that they suggest
To signal that your answer is below the standard they expect
To see how you respond under pressure, while applying the same criteria to everyone
To make the process harder for candidates they have a poor impression of

questions.hint: Challenge is often a deliberate test of composure and influence.

questions.prompt: In a video interview, a panellist keeps their camera off. Where should you look while speaking?

options.text: At your prepared notes, so that you do not lose your place
At the panellist's name box, so that you can see their reaction
At the camera, pausing slightly between sentences
At your own image, so that you can check how you appear to them

questions.hint: Looking at the camera gives the impression of eye contact.

questions.prompt: Your audio fails during an answer in a remote interview. What should you do?

options.text: End the call and rejoin without explaining why
Wait quietly until the panel notices there is a problem
Tell the panel at once and ask where they last heard you
Carry on speaking in case the sound returns by itself

questions.hint: Saying so promptly avoids lost evidence.

questions.prompt: A panellist from another department is on the panel. What is the best adjustment?

options.text: Avoid your own department's acronyms and explain technical terms
Address your answers to the colleagues from your own department, who will follow them
Use your usual vocabulary, as an experienced panellist will pick it up quickly
Simplify the content of your answers as well as the language

questions.hint: Panellists from outside may not know your terms.

questions.prompt: Which question would a panel not normally be allowed to ask?

options.text: Whether you plan to have children
Whether you can work at the location stated in the advert
Whether you can meet the security clearance requirements for the role
Whether you have experience of managing a budget

questions.hint: Questions on family plans have no place in a merit-based process.

questions.prompt: A panellist asks an inappropriate question. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: End the interview at that point and report it the same day
Challenge the panellist directly during the interview, so that they withdraw the question
Steer the answer politely to the skills the role needs and raise it afterwards with the recruiter
Answer it fully, so that you do not appear unco-operative with the panel

questions.hint: You can keep the focus on the role and report it later.

questions.prompt: Which principle explains why panels stay neutral and ask each candidate the same questions?

options.text: They must avoid encouraging candidates during the interview
They must avoid eye contact so that they are not influenced
They must apply the same criteria consistently to every candidate
They must not take notes while a candidate is speaking

questions.hint: Consistent treatment is part of fair, open competition.

questions.prompt: A panellist joins the video call five minutes late. What is the best reaction?

options.text: Restart your answer so that the late panellist hears it all
Ask the late panellist to explain why they were not on time
Stop and wait for them to settle before going on
Carry on calmly and let the chair decide whether to recap

questions.hint: The chair manages late joiners; staying composed is the priority.

items.title: L12: Strengths questions for HEO roles
items.body:
At HEO and above, strengths questions probe how you lead, decide and behave when the work is hard. The panel wants to hear what energises you, but also how you behave when you are not doing what you enjoy. Typical questions include: 'What do you do when your team is behind with a deadline?', 'Which part of managing people do you find most draining?', and 'What would your team say about you?'

Two points matter at this level. First, strengths can be overplayed. A strong preference for detail can slow decisions, and a love of helping can mean you take on too much. Showing that you know how a strength can go wrong, and that you manage it, signals maturity. Second, the panel will compare what you say with the role. If you say you most enjoy working alone on analysis, but the role is mainly about leading and negotiating, the mismatch will show.

Strengths answers are short, so aim for a clear claim, a reason and an example. 'I enjoy getting people to see the point of a change. In my last team, I held a short session to explain why the new process mattered and then asked people what would get in their way.' That is more convincing than 'I am a great communicator'.

Expect rapid-fire formats. The panel may ask a series of questions with little time between them, and some include 'either-or' forced choices: 'Would you rather finish a piece of work to a high standard or deliver it on time?' Answer honestly, with a reason, and say how you would reduce the downside of the choice. Where energy is part of what is scored, stay warm and engaged all the way through, including at the end of a long interview.

questions.prompt: What does a panel mainly want to learn from a strengths question about what drains you?

options.text: Which tasks you would refuse to do in the role
How you behave when doing work you enjoy less, and how you manage it
How long you can work without needing a break
Whether you will criticise your current manager when asked

questions.hint: Self-awareness and management of lower-energy tasks are being tested.

questions.prompt: What does it mean to say a strength can be overplayed?

options.text: Used too much, it can cause problems, such as a love of detail slowing decisions
A strength is exaggerated in the panel's eyes if you use superlatives
A strength you mention too often will be viewed with suspicion
A strength fades over time unless you use it regularly

questions.hint: Showing awareness of the downside signals maturity.

questions.prompt: The role is mainly about negotiating with partners. A candidate says they most enjoy working alone on analysis. What is the effect?

options.text: The panel may see a mismatch between the candidate's energy and the job
The panel will see the candidate as thorough and so well suited to the role
The panel will treat the answer as irrelevant to the scoring
The panel will ask the candidate to give a different answer

questions.hint: Panels compare strengths with the demands of the role.

questions.prompt: Which answer is the most convincing to 'What are you good at?'

options.text: I am good at all of the things the job requires, and I am keen to prove it
I am a great communicator and my team often tell me so, which is why they come to me first
I like helping people see why a change matters; last year I ran a short session and asked what would get in their way
I enjoy working with people and I think I am approachable and easy to talk to

questions.hint: A claim backed by a short, specific example is more credible.

questions.prompt: Asked, 'Would you rather finish to a high standard or deliver on time?', what is the best approach?

options.text: Say that you would do both and that there is no real trade-off
Choose one honestly, give a reason and say how you would limit the downside
Choose delivery on time, since that is what the Civil Service prefers
Say that it depends and leave it there, since the panel gave no detail

questions.hint: Honest choices with mitigation show insight.

questions.prompt: Why can the end of a long strengths interview be tricky?

options.text: The panel gives extra marks for the final question
The questions become harder as the interview goes on
The panel will have decided already and so stop listening
Energy is part of what is scored, so you must stay engaged to the last question

questions.hint: Energy and enthusiasm are scored throughout.

questions.prompt: What is a sound way to identify your strengths if you are unsure?

options.text: Ask colleagues what they come to you for and notice the work you volunteer for
Read the strengths listed in the job advert and choose the ones that fit
Ask a friend to write a list of your strengths for you
Take an online personality test and quote the result to the panel

questions.hint: Evidence from others and your own choices shows real strengths.

questions.prompt: A panel asks, 'What would your team say about you?' Which answer is best?

options.text: They would say that I am hardworking, approachable and always willing to help
They would say that I always make sure they have what they need
They would say that I am a very good manager and a great person to work for
They would say I explain why work matters and give them room to decide how, though I can be slow to let go of detail

questions.hint: A balanced, specific answer shows self-awareness.

questions.prompt: In a strengths interview a candidate gives one-word answers. What is missing?

options.text: A reason and an example to show that the claim is real
A link to the department's values
An apology for the brevity of the answers
Longer pauses between answers, to show thought

questions.hint: Strengths answers need a claim, a reason and an example.

questions.prompt: How should you answer, 'What do you do when your team is behind on a deadline?'

options.text: Say that you would give the work to whoever is quickest
Say that you would ask your manager to extend the deadline
Say that you would work longer hours yourself, to catch up
Describe how you would assess the position, reprioritise and support the team

questions.hint: It shows leadership, prioritising and supporting people.

items.title: L12: Leading a team through change
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Behaviours - Leadership, Changing and Improving, Managing a Quality Service (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Interviews for HEO roles often ask for an example of leading a team through change, such as a restructure, a new system or a changed priority. The question usually draws on Leadership, and sometimes Changing and Improving or Managing a Quality Service. Panels want to see that you can bring others with you, not simply implement a plan.

A strong example covers four things. First, how you understood the change and what it meant for your team, including the people who stood to lose most. Second, how you communicated: explaining why the change was happening, being honest about what you did not yet know, and giving people a chance to ask questions and raise concerns. Third, what you did to support people, such as training, adjusting workloads, giving individuals time to adapt or arranging one-to-ones. Fourth, how you kept the service going during the change and how you checked that it worked, for example through error rates, customer feedback or team morale.

Resistance is normal and a good example describes it honestly. People may worry about their jobs, workloads or skills. A strong answer shows you listening to the concern, responding to what could be changed and being clear about what could not. Avoid describing resistant colleagues as obstacles.

Be precise about your role. If a senior manager decided on the change, say so, and focus on what you decided: how it was introduced to your team, how you sequenced it and how you kept standards. Also mention any risks you managed, such as backlogs during a system switch.

Finally, evaluate honestly. Say what worked, what you would do differently and what you learned. For instance, you might have consulted staff earlier or tested the new system with a small group first.

questions.prompt: Which part of a change-leadership answer best shows you can bring people with you?

options.text: The date by which you completed the roll-out, since meeting the deadline shows control of the programme
How you explained why the change was happening and listened to concerns
The number of staff affected, since a larger change shows greater leadership responsibility
The seniority of the sponsor you reported to, since it shows how important the change was

questions.hint: Communication and listening show people were brought along.

questions.prompt: A colleague worries about losing duties in a restructure. Which response is most effective?

options.text: Listen, be honest about what is and is not decided and agree how you will support them
Tell them the decision was made above your level and that you cannot explain the reasons behind it
Reassure them that nothing will change for them, so that morale stays steady while the restructure goes ahead
Move their work to colleagues who are less anxious, so that the uncertainty does not slow the team

questions.hint: Honesty and support build trust through change.

questions.prompt: A candidate calls resistant colleagues 'obstacles'. What is the issue?

options.text: It is acceptable as long as the change was delivered successfully, because outcomes matter most
It shows frustration with the senior team that set the change, which a panel may read as disloyalty
It makes the example sound harder than it was, which weakens the evidence of your own effort
It suggests they did not try to understand people's concerns

questions.hint: Panels look for listening, not labelling.

questions.prompt: A senior manager decided on a system change. What should your answer concentrate on?

options.text: What the department planned for the other teams, as it shows you understand the wider programme
What you decided on introduction, sequencing and keeping standards in your team
Which system was chosen and what it could do, as the detail shows you understood what was introduced
Why the senior manager's decision was the right one, since panels want to see you back leadership decisions

questions.hint: Panels score your own actions.

questions.prompt: During a system switch, backlogs rise. Which action best shows managing a quality service?

options.text: Ask the team to work through their breaks until the backlog clears, which shows personal commitment
Monitor the backlog, prioritise urgent cases and agree a recovery plan
Report the backlog to your manager and wait for instruction before changing how the team works
Delay customer replies until the system settles, so that quality is not harmed by rushed answers

questions.hint: Active management of service quality shows the Behaviour.

questions.prompt: How could you best show the change worked?

options.text: Say that nobody raised a complaint afterwards, which shows the change was accepted by the team
State that the project finished on time and within the approved budget, which shows delivery
Cite a measure such as error rate or customer feedback, with an account of team morale
Say the senior manager was pleased with the outcome and that other teams later copied the approach

questions.hint: Measures and feedback provide evidence of impact.

questions.prompt: What does an honest evaluation add to a change answer?

options.text: What you would do differently, such as consulting staff earlier
A statement that every target was met, because panels give most credit to clean results
A defence of every decision you made along the way, so the panel sees your judgement was sound throughout
A list of the problems caused by other teams, so the panel understands the difficulties you faced

questions.hint: Reflection shows learning and credibility.

questions.prompt: Why might you test a new system with a small group first?

options.text: It lets the pilot group take the credit for the change, which improves buy-in across the wider team
It reveals problems before the whole team is affected
It makes the programme look more complicated, which suggests to the panel that you are thorough
It avoids the need for training later, because the pilot group will teach the others informally

questions.hint: Piloting reduces risk.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes how resistance to change should be treated?

options.text: As an attitude problem in the individual, to be dealt with through the performance process
As a sign that the change should be paused until everybody is in agreement about how it will work
As a normal reaction that can provide useful information
As a matter best left to HR, since a manager's job is to deliver the change rather than discuss it

questions.hint: Resistance often highlights real risks.

questions.prompt: What is a weakness to avoid in a change answer?

options.text: Mentioning the risks that you managed along the way
Describing difficulties with the change openly and honestly
Saying what you learned from the experience of the change
Describing only the plan and not what you did with people

questions.hint: A plan alone is not evidence of leadership.

items.title: L12: Difficult conversations and conflict within a team
items.source: ACAS guidance on managing conflict and Civil Service Success Profiles: Working Together (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Managers are often asked how they handle conflict between colleagues, challenging feedback or a team member who is not meeting expectations. Panels use these questions to test fairness, courage and judgement. They also reveal how you treat confidential matters, so avoid naming people.

A reliable approach to a difficult conversation is to prepare, then hold it promptly and privately. Prepare by getting the facts straight: what specifically happened, when, and with what effect. Decide the outcome you want and think about how the other person might see it. In the conversation, describe the behaviour and its impact rather than labelling the person: 'In the last two meetings you interrupted colleagues, and two people have said they no longer contribute' is better than 'You are rude'. Then invite their view, listen without interrupting and look for causes. Agree what will happen next, with a date to review, and follow it up in writing where appropriate.

In a conflict between two colleagues, a manager usually speaks to each separately first to understand their perspective, then brings them together if appropriate to agree how to work together. A manager should be impartial, stay focused on behaviours and the work, and avoid taking sides. Where the conflict has become bullying, harassment or discrimination, it should be dealt with under the department's formal procedures, and the manager should seek advice from HR.

A common weakness is delay: waiting in the hope that a problem resolves itself usually makes it worse. Another is overcorrecting, so that a manager becomes confrontational. Panels like to hear that you were firm and fair and that the relationship survived.

Be ready to say what you would do differently. Maybe you would have intervened earlier, or you would have asked more questions before forming a view.

questions.prompt: What should you do first when preparing a difficult conversation with a team member?

options.text: Plan what you will say if they become angry, so that you stay in control of the discussion
Decide how severe a sanction should be, so that the conversation has a clear and firm purpose
Get the facts straight: what happened, when and with what effect
Ask other colleagues what they think of the person, so that you hear a range of views

questions.hint: Evidence-based preparation keeps the conversation fair and specific.

questions.prompt: Which statement describes behaviour and impact rather than labelling the person?

options.text: You need to be more of a team player, and I would like you to work on that
You have an attitude problem in meetings, and people have started to notice it
You are rude, and it is affecting the team, so I need you to stop it from now on
In the last two meetings you interrupted colleagues, and two people have said they no longer contribute

questions.hint: Specific observations are easier to discuss and less likely to provoke defensiveness.

questions.prompt: Two colleagues are in conflict. What does a manager usually do first?

options.text: Move one of them to a different team, so that the conflict ends quickly and work can continue
Bring them together at once to settle it, so that each hears the other's version first-hand
Tell them both to resolve it themselves, as adults, and to come back if they cannot
Speak to each separately to understand their perspective

questions.hint: Hearing each side privately gives you facts before a joint conversation.

questions.prompt: Why does a manager need to stay impartial in a dispute between colleagues?

options.text: To keep the focus on behaviour and work and to be seen as fair
To avoid having to involve HR, which would formalise a matter that can be settled informally
To keep the matter informal, so that neither colleague feels that they are being judged
To protect their own position, since taking sides could lead to a complaint against them

questions.hint: Impartiality maintains trust.

questions.prompt: When should a conflict be handled through formal procedures with HR advice?

options.text: When one of the colleagues asks for it, as the manager must always follow their wishes
When the manager feels uncomfortable, since informal handling then carries a higher risk
When it involves bullying, harassment or discrimination
When it has lasted more than a week, as a longer dispute needs a more formal response

questions.hint: Serious conduct matters need formal handling.

questions.prompt: A manager delays a difficult conversation, hoping the issue will resolve. What is the usual result?

options.text: The employee takes the silence as approval, which makes later feedback seem unfair to them
The panel will see it as a patient approach, because managers should give people time to improve
The problem tends to grow and become harder to address
The problem goes away on its own, and the employee appreciates not being criticised in the meantime

questions.hint: Delay usually makes a problem worse.

questions.prompt: How should you describe a conflict case in an interview?

options.text: By blaming the person who caused the difficulty, so that the panel sees why action was needed
Without naming individuals, and focusing on your own actions
Using names, so that the panel can see exactly who was involved and judge how serious the case was
In very general terms, with no description of what you did, so that nobody can be identified

questions.hint: Confidentiality and your own actions both matter.

questions.prompt: Which description of the outcome is strongest?

options.text: The conflict ended after I spoke to both colleagues, and everybody was happy with the result
The problem was passed to HR, who resolved it, and I was not involved again
The two colleagues agreed how to share the work and we reviewed it after a month; collaboration improved
Both colleagues were happy in the end, and the team was never affected by the conflict

questions.hint: Specific results and follow-up demonstrate success.

questions.prompt: What risk comes from overcorrecting in a difficult conversation?

options.text: The manager shows too much empathy, so the employee does not understand how serious the matter is
The employee loses interest in the conversation, since firm handling makes people stop listening
The conversation is too short to cover the facts, because a firm manner leaves little room for views
The manager becomes confrontational and damages the relationship

questions.hint: Firm and fair is better than harsh.

questions.prompt: What is an effective closing step for a difficult conversation?

options.text: Ask the colleague to write down what they have heard, so that nothing is misunderstood later
Say that you will think about what was said and get back to them when you have decided what to do
Tell the colleague to expect another meeting at some point, so that they are aware it is not finished
Agree what will happen next, with a date to review progress

questions.hint: Agreed next steps and a review date make the conversation meaningful.

items.title: L12: Layered probes and hypothetical follow-ups
items.body:
At HEO level, panels often layer their questions. After you have told your example, they test it with a series of further questions that become more demanding: first a clarifying probe ('What was your role?'), then a reasoning probe ('Why did you choose that?'), and then a challenge or hypothetical ('What if the budget had been cut halfway through?' or 'How would you have handled it if the stakeholder had refused?').

The layers have a purpose. The first set confirms that the example is real and yours. The second tests your judgement. The third tests whether you can apply what you did to a new situation. Answers to hypotheticals should be consistent with the values and approach that your example showed. If you describe yourself as consultative, a hypothetical in which you would impose a decision without discussion will undermine the credibility of your example.

When the hypothetical is unfamiliar, use the same method every time. State what you would want to know first, name the options, decide which you would choose and why, and say how you would check that it was working. This is better than jumping straight to an answer.

Be careful not to treat a hypothetical as an invitation to change the facts of your story. 'If that had happened, I would have done the same, because...' is better than inventing a new version of events. You can say honestly when something did not happen and describe how you would adapt your approach.

If a probe suggests you made a mistake, acknowledge it directly. A candidate who says 'That was a weakness in how I planned it, and I now do X' scores better than one who defends the original choice at all costs.

questions.prompt: Which sequence best describes the layers of a probing sequence on one example?

options.text: Checking your dates, then your job title, then your pay and responsibilities at the time
Clarifying your role, testing your reasoning, then testing how you would apply it to a new situation
Confirming your qualifications, then your references, then your reasons for leaving the role
Repeating the original question, testing your memory of detail, then testing your nerves

questions.hint: Each layer tests a more demanding aspect of your example.

questions.prompt: Why must a hypothetical answer be consistent with the example you gave?

options.text: Inconsistency suggests the example did not honestly reflect how you work
Hypothetical answers are scored under a separate Behaviour from the example
Panels automatically mark an answer lower if it differs from the first one
The panel has already written notes on the example and cannot change them

questions.hint: Consistency supports credibility.

questions.prompt: You described a consultative approach. The panel asks what you would do if a stakeholder refused to engage. Which reply fits?

options.text: Make the decision without them and tell them afterwards, to keep the work moving
Say that the situation would never arise, because consultation prevents refusals
Ask your manager to take over the relationship, because it has clearly broken down
Try to understand their concerns, offer alternatives and escalate only if needed

questions.hint: It stays consistent with a consultative approach while recognising limits.

questions.prompt: Which approach works best for an unfamiliar hypothetical?

options.text: Give a quick, decisive answer so that you appear confident about the situation
State what you would need to know, set out options, choose one with reasons and say how you would check it
Apply the same answer you gave in your example, since it worked then
Say that it depends and ask the panel for more details before answering

questions.hint: A repeatable method shows structured thinking.

questions.prompt: The panel asks, 'What if the budget had been halved?' Which mistake should you avoid?

options.text: Rewriting your story so that it never happened the way you first described it
Acknowledging the effect on delivery
Explaining how you would reprioritise the work
Saying what you would protect first

questions.hint: The hypothetical is a new scenario, not a chance to change the facts.

questions.prompt: A probe reveals a flaw in your plan. What is the strongest response?

options.text: Defend the plan and explain why it was reasonable at the time
Say that circumstances changed after the plan was agreed
Say that others approved the plan before it went ahead
Acknowledge it directly and say what you do differently now

questions.hint: Owning the mistake shows learning.

questions.prompt: Why should you keep each answer brief during layered probing?

options.text: The panel prefers one-word answers to full explanations
Short answers always signal confidence to a panel
Each layer of probing is timed separately and cut off
Long answers use up time and limit the later questions that carry marks

questions.hint: Time is limited and later probes carry marks.

questions.prompt: Which probe tests your reasoning most directly?

options.text: How long did the work take?
When did you start?
Why did you choose that approach rather than the alternatives?
Who else was involved in the work?

questions.hint: It asks for the thinking behind the choice.

questions.prompt: Which question is an example of a hypothetical probe?

options.text: How did the project end, and what was the final cost?
What was your own role in the project from start to finish?
Which department were you working in at the time?
How would you have handled it if your sponsor had withdrawn support halfway through?

questions.hint: Hypotheticals ask about situations that did not happen.

questions.prompt: How should you respond to a probe about something that did not happen in your example?

options.text: Say that you cannot answer and ask for another question
Say it did not happen and describe how you would adapt your approach
Describe it as if it had happened, so that the answer sounds complete
Switch to a different example in which it did happen

questions.hint: Honest handling keeps credibility.

items.title: L12: Putting numbers and boundaries on your own contribution
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles: Behaviours (GOV.UK); Civil Service Code (honesty)
items.body:
When a team achievement is described, panels need to know where your contribution begins and ends. At EO and HEO this is harder than it sounds, because senior grades often work through others and share credit. The aim is a precise, honest account that neither hides nor inflates your role.

One method is to separate four things: the objective (what the team set out to achieve), the decision you made, the actions you took yourself, and the actions others took because of your direction. For example: 'The objective was to cut processing time. I analysed the case data, decided to move triage to the front of the process and briefed the team. Two colleagues built the new checklist under my direction, and the team's average time dropped from eight days to five.' That account is generous to others and clear about you.

Be specific about scale. Use figures where you have them: team size, budget, caseload, time saved. If you do not know the exact number, give an honest approximation and say it is approximate. Do not claim a percentage unless you can explain how it was measured.

Where the achievement is shared, say how. If two of you ran a project, state which parts each led. If a manager set the objective and you delivered it, say so. Panels commonly ask, 'What would your manager say your contribution was?' and your answer should match what they would say.

Also be alert to the opposite mistake, which is excessive modesty. 'I just did what I was asked' gives the panel nothing to score. Describe decisions that were yours, including trade-offs you weighed, and results that your decisions produced.

Finally, honesty matters. The Civil Service Code requires honesty, and an inflated account can be exposed by probes, references and pre-employment checks.

questions.prompt: Which four elements help you define your own contribution to a team achievement?

options.text: The objective, your decision, your own actions and what others did under your direction
The cost, the date, the location and the size of the team, since these give the panel the scale of the work
The problem, the plan, the risk and the review, since these show how a project is managed from start to finish
The sponsor, the budget, the programme and the outcome, since these are the facts panels expect to hear

questions.hint: These separate your role from the team's.

questions.prompt: A candidate says, 'The team's processing time fell from eight days to five.' What is missing?

options.text: An explanation of how the time was measured, so that the figures can be checked
What they decided and did to bring about the improvement
The date on which the change took effect, so that the panel can judge how recent the example is
The names of the team members who took part, so the panel can follow who did what

questions.hint: Panels score personal contribution.

questions.prompt: You do not know the exact figure for time saved. What is the best course?

options.text: Say you cannot give any figure at all, because a wrong number would be worse than none
Leave the figure out and describe the benefit in general terms, so that nothing can be challenged
Give an honest approximation and say it is approximate
Quote a precise figure that sounds right, so that the panel is satisfied and does not probe further

questions.hint: Honest approximation is acceptable and credible.

questions.prompt: Two people ran a project jointly. How should you describe your part?

options.text: State which parts you led and which your colleague led
Describe only the outcome, so that the question of who did what does not come up
Describe it as your project with some help from a colleague, since you were the person who took the lead
Say that you shared everything equally, so that nobody can say you took the credit for the work

questions.hint: Clear attribution is honest and still shows your role.

questions.prompt: The panel asks what your manager would say your contribution was. What should you aim for?

options.text: An answer that quotes your manager's praise, since a senior view carries more weight than your own
An answer that matches what your manager would genuinely say
An answer that makes your contribution sound bigger, since the panel expects candidates to sell themselves
An answer that avoids mentioning your manager, since the panel is scoring you and not them

questions.hint: Panels may check the answer through references.

questions.prompt: Which statement shows excessive modesty?

options.text: I briefed the team on the change and answered questions on how it would work for each of them
I analysed the case data and found that most of the delay arose at a single approval step
I just did what I was asked
I decided to move triage to the front of the process, as the data showed that the delays began there

questions.hint: Modesty that hides decisions gives the panel nothing to score.

questions.prompt: Why is it a risk to claim a percentage improvement without explanation?

options.text: Percentages are never accepted as evidence at interview, because panels prefer short, plain descriptions
The panel may ask how it was measured and you may not be able to say
It makes the answer too short to be scored, since the panel needs a longer account of what happened
It suggests you are a statistician rather than a manager, which does not suit a leadership answer

questions.hint: Claims need to be explained and honest.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is both generous to others and clear about your own role?

options.text: Two colleagues built the checklist under my direction after I decided to change the triage point
My team deserve the credit for this, as they did the hard work and I only supported them
I did everything necessary to make it happen, from analysis through to the training of the team
The team worked really well together, and the improvement shows what we can do when we collaborate

questions.hint: It names others' actions and your decision.

questions.prompt: Which Civil Service Code value is most relevant to an inflated account of your contribution?

options.text: Integrity in handling public money, because overclaiming is a form of fraud
Objectivity, because decisions must be based on analysis of the evidence
Honesty
Impartiality, because a candidate must not favour their own account over the facts

questions.hint: Honesty means being truthful and not misleading others.

questions.prompt: Where might an inflated account be exposed?

options.text: Only at the final stage of recruitment, when the successful candidate's file is reviewed
Only if one of the panel happens to know your team and can compare it with your account
In probes, references and pre-employment checks
It would not be exposed, as panels have no way to check what a candidate says

questions.hint: Claims are checked in several ways.

items.title: L12: Case studies: stakeholders, options and risk
items.source: HM Treasury Green Book (appraisal and options) and Civil Service Success Profiles (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Case-study exercises at HEO level often require you to weigh options for a service or policy with several stakeholders who want different things. A useful method has five steps.

First, clarify the objective: what is the change meant to achieve, for whom, by when, and with what budget? Without a clear objective, you cannot judge options.

Second, map stakeholders. Identify who is affected, who has influence and what each wants. Do not assume the most senior person is the only one who matters. Service users, front-line staff, partner organisations and finance or legal colleagues may all be critical. A simple grid of influence against interest helps decide how to engage each one.

Third, set out options. The HM Treasury Green Book, the government's guidance on appraisal, recommends a 'do nothing' or business-as-usual baseline against which other options are compared, and a shortlist of realistic options. Compare them against criteria drawn from the objective, such as cost, benefit to users, deliverability and risk. Show the criteria and your reasons openly.

Fourth, assess risk. Identify what could go wrong, how likely it is, how serious it would be and what you would do about it. The Green Book also warns of optimism bias, the tendency to be too hopeful about costs and timescales, so test assumptions and allow contingency.

Fifth, recommend and plan. Choose an option, explain why it beats the others, and describe how you would communicate it to each stakeholder group and measure success.

Throughout, remember public money must be spent with regard to propriety and value for money. If a stakeholder's request would favour one provider unfairly, say how you would handle it.

questions.prompt: What should be established first in a case study involving several stakeholders?

options.text: Which option is cheapest, since public money must be spent with value for money in mind
The objective: what the change must achieve, for whom, by when and with what budget
What the department did in a similar case, since precedent shows what will be accepted
Which stakeholder has the most senior role, since their view will decide which option is chosen

questions.hint: Without a clear objective, options cannot be judged.

questions.prompt: Which tool helps decide how to engage each stakeholder?

options.text: A list of the stakeholders' names in alphabetical order, so that nobody is overlooked
A calendar of meetings with each stakeholder, so that you can plan when each will be consulted
A table of the salary bands of each stakeholder, so that you know who has the authority to decide
A grid of influence against interest

questions.hint: It sorts stakeholders by power and concern.

questions.prompt: Why does the Green Book recommend a 'do nothing' or business-as-usual baseline?

options.text: It provides a point of comparison for the other options
It shows that doing nothing is the cheapest option, so any change must justify its extra cost
It is always the preferred option unless the other options clearly beat it on cost
It allows the project to be postponed while more information is gathered about the other options

questions.hint: Options are judged against the baseline.

questions.prompt: Which criteria should options be compared against?

options.text: Criteria based on how popular each option is with staff, because acceptance affects delivery
Criteria drawn from the objective, such as cost, user benefit, deliverability and risk
Criteria chosen to favour the cheapest option, because cost is the one measure that can be checked
Criteria set by the most senior stakeholder, because they are the person who will decide

questions.hint: Criteria linked to the objective make the comparison fair.

questions.prompt: What does optimism bias refer to?

options.text: Being too hopeful about costs and timescales
Preferring options that give the decision-maker the most choice, even if they cost more
Assuming that every stakeholder will support the change once its benefits have been explained
Being too negative about outcomes, so that costs are overstated and benefits are understated

questions.hint: The Green Book warns of underestimating costs and time.

questions.prompt: How should optimism bias be dealt with in a case study?

options.text: Ignore any risks that are unlikely, so that the analysis stays focused on the likeliest outcomes
Test assumptions and allow contingency
Rely on the project sponsor's estimates, because they know the work better than anyone else does
Add a flat percentage to every figure, whatever the evidence, so that the estimate is always on the safe side

questions.hint: Challenging assumptions guards against it.

questions.prompt: Which element completes a risk assessment?

options.text: Likelihood, impact and what you would do about each risk
The total number of risks identified, so that the reader can see how thorough the work has been
A single overall risk rating for the whole project, so that the decision-maker has one figure to use
The names of the people who raised each risk and the date it was identified, so that it can be traced

questions.hint: A risk needs a response.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder suggests giving the contract to a favoured supplier without competition. What should you do?

options.text: Ignore the request and carry on with the planned process, hoping that they will drop it
Explain the need for fair and open procurement and propose a compliant route
Accept the request because of their seniority, since they are likely to have checked the rules already
Delay the project until they change their mind, so that you do not have to make the decision

questions.hint: Public money must be spent with propriety.

questions.prompt: What should a recommendation include?

options.text: The chosen option, why it beats the others and how success would be measured
A list of all the options considered, with a short note on each, so that the reader can choose
A summary of the stakeholders' views, so that the decision-maker knows who supports what
A statement that the decision is for ministers, so that your own view does not influence it

questions.hint: It must be justified and measurable.

questions.prompt: Which communication approach is best?

options.text: Wait until the decision is final before telling any stakeholder, so that the message is clear
Send the same message to every group, so that nobody feels they have been given a different account
Tailor messages to each stakeholder group's concerns
Communicate only with the sponsor, who can then pass the message on to everyone else

questions.hint: Different groups need different messages.

items.title: L12: In-tray exercises with conflict, delegation and confidentiality
items.source: Civil Service Jobs candidate guidance and Civil Service Code (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Advanced in-tray exercises include items that conflict with each other, items that need delegation and items that carry a hidden ethical issue. The assessors are looking for a calm, reasoned approach rather than a perfect order of tasks.

To handle conflicting demands, first check whether the conflict is real. Two requests may be compatible if one is done earlier or by someone else. If it is real, decide on impact: which failure would cost more, to the public, to the department or to a person's wellbeing? Then tell both requesters, explain your decision and offer an alternative. Silently dropping one request is poor practice because the requester may be relying on it.

Delegation is about matching tasks to people. Consider skill, capacity and development. Give a clear brief covering what is needed, by when, the standard expected and who to ask if stuck. Agree a check-in point. Remember that delegating a task does not delegate accountability: you remain responsible for the outcome. Some matters, such as a personal data breach or a possible conflict of interest, should be escalated rather than delegated.

Confidentiality traps are common. An email may be copied to the wrong people, a colleague may ask you to share a file with personal data outside the department, or a request may ask you to reveal the content of a colleague's grievance. The Civil Service Code requires integrity and honesty, and data protection rules require personal data to be handled securely and shared only where there is a lawful reason. If in doubt, do not share and seek advice from the appropriate person, such as the data protection officer.

questions.prompt: Two requests appear to conflict. What should you check first?

options.text: Whether the conflict is real, or whether the tasks can be done in sequence or by others
Which sender has the higher grade, since their request carries more weight in the department
Which request is easier to complete, since quick wins reduce the pressure from the in-tray
Which request arrived first, since fairness means dealing with items in the order received

questions.hint: Many apparent conflicts can be resolved.

questions.prompt: When two demands do conflict, how should you decide between them?

options.text: By working on whichever is quicker, since this clears the most items before the time runs out
By choosing the request from the more senior person, since they are likely to have the wider view
By waiting to see whether the two requesters resolve it themselves, so that you avoid taking sides
By comparing the impact of each failing, then telling both requesters

questions.hint: Decisions based on impact are defensible.

questions.prompt: Which brief makes a delegated task most likely to succeed?

options.text: The task title and a deadline, since a capable colleague will work out the rest
What is needed, by when, to what standard and who to ask if stuck
A request to report back when it is finished, so that you can check the result
A copy of the whole email chain, so that the colleague has all of the background

questions.hint: Clear briefs support delivery.

questions.prompt: If you delegate a task to a colleague, who remains accountable for the outcome?

options.text: The colleague, because they now own the task and its result
You
The sponsor of the project, because they set the objective
Your manager, because they oversee the work of the team as a whole

questions.hint: Accountability is not delegated.

questions.prompt: Which matter should be escalated rather than delegated?

options.text: A diary clash between two meetings, because the person who accepted both must resolve it
A personal data breach
A routine reply to a customer who has asked about progress, because it can be answered quickly
A booking for a meeting room, because it affects other people's use of the building

questions.hint: Serious matters need senior or specialist handling.

questions.prompt: A colleague asks you to send personal data on service users to an outside contact by personal email. What should you do?

options.text: Send it, because a senior colleague has asked and will have confirmed that it is allowed
Forward the request to your manager and wait, without telling the colleague what you have done
Decline to send it that way and ask the data protection officer for the right route
Send it with a password on the file, so that the information is protected in transit

questions.hint: Personal data must be shared only securely and with lawful reason.

questions.prompt: A request asks you to reveal the details of a colleague's grievance. What is right?

options.text: Ignore the request and say nothing, so that no one can say you handled it wrongly
Decline and refer the request to the right person in HR
Share the details with the wider team, so that everybody knows how to avoid the same issue
Share a short summary with the requester, leaving out names so that nobody can be identified

questions.hint: Grievance details are confidential.

questions.prompt: Why explain your reasoning after an in-tray exercise?

options.text: It shows you used sound criteria, and that matters more than the exact order
It is the only part of the exercise that is scored, so the written answers carry little weight
It lets you change the answers you gave on the day, since the panel will give credit for later thought
It makes the interview longer, which gives you more time to show the strengths of your approach

questions.hint: Reasoning shows judgement.

questions.prompt: Which approach to a dropped request is poor practice?

options.text: Silently dropping one without telling the requester
Telling the requester and offering an alternative date or a different person to help
Asking for an extension of the deadline from the requester, with reasons
Proposing that a colleague takes over the task, and explaining why

questions.hint: Requesters may be relying on you.

questions.prompt: What should you agree with someone to whom you delegate?

options.text: A private email address for the colleague, so that they can reach you out of hours
A check-in point
A new job title for the colleague, so that they have the authority to complete the task
A pay rise for the colleague, since the task is more demanding than their usual work

questions.hint: A check-in supports quality.

items.title: L12: Challenging questions: weaknesses, failure and 'why you?'
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles and Civil Service Jobs candidate guidance (GOV.UK)
items.body:
Some questions put you on the spot: 'What is your biggest weakness?', 'Tell us about a time you failed', 'Why should we choose you over an internal candidate?', or 'What would you do if you did not get the job?' They look hard, but each can be answered with a simple method.

For weaknesses and failures, choose something real but not fatal to the role. Say what it was, what the effect was, what you did and what has changed. For example, a candidate might say they used to hold on to tasks instead of delegating, noticed that it made the team slow, and now sets a weekly review to hand over work. Avoid disguised strengths ('I work too hard') and avoid weaknesses that are central to the job. The panel wants to see insight and development, not perfection.

For failure, own it. Describe your role honestly, avoid blaming others and show what you learned and how you applied it. A failure from earlier in your career is acceptable if you show the lesson carried forward.

For 'why you?', do not criticise other candidates. You do not know them. Focus on the evidence that you meet the criteria: your results, your relevant experience and what you would bring. If you are an internal candidate, show that you also look beyond your current team.

If asked what you would do if unsuccessful, give an honest, constructive answer. You would ask for feedback, work on development areas and apply again when ready. A response that shows resilience and a commitment to the Civil Service is better than one which suggests you would leave.

Whatever the question, a short pause, a clear structure and honesty are your best tools. If a question is truly inappropriate, steer politely back to the role.

questions.prompt: Which is the best choice of weakness to discuss?

options.text: A strength that sounds like a weakness, such as being a perfectionist, so that it shows you in a good light
A real one that is not central to the role, with the steps you have taken to improve
A weakness that is central to the job but that you think is minor, so that the answer is honest
Something that you have never been criticised for, so that nobody can dispute your account

questions.hint: Real, manageable weaknesses show insight.

questions.prompt: A candidate says, 'My weakness is that I work too hard.' What is the problem?

options.text: It is too specific, because a weakness should be described in general terms
It is too honest, because panels prefer candidates who do not discuss weaknesses
It is too personal, because the panel is only interested in work skills
It is a disguised strength and shows a lack of self-awareness

questions.hint: Panels dislike clichés.

questions.prompt: Which structure works for a weakness question?

options.text: What it was, the effect, what you did and what has changed
The cause, the person to blame and the penalty that you received, so the account is complete
The date, the place and the people involved, so the panel can picture the situation clearly
The excuse that you offered at the time, the lesson learned and the final outcome of the matter

questions.hint: Insight and development are the focus.

questions.prompt: When describing a failure, what matters most?

options.text: Owning your part and showing what you learned and applied
Explaining why the failure was not your fault, so that the panel sees you are not careless
Showing that the failure was widely shared, so that the blame is spread across the team
Showing that the failure was minor, so that the panel is not worried about your judgement

questions.hint: Responsibility and learning matter.

questions.prompt: Which view of an earlier-career failure is correct?

options.text: It is acceptable only if the failure was small, because a major failure counts against you
It is acceptable if you show the lesson carried forward
It is acceptable only if the panel knows you, because they can then judge it for themselves
It is not acceptable, because anything that old no longer reflects how you work

questions.hint: The lesson is the point.

questions.prompt: Asked, 'Why should we choose you over an internal candidate?', what is the best approach?

options.text: Focus on your evidence against the criteria without criticising others
Explain what the other candidates lack, so that the panel understands why you are the stronger choice
Say you have more experience than any other candidate, since length of service shows commitment
Say that the panel should take a risk on you, since fresh thinking is what the team needs

questions.hint: You do not know the other candidates.

questions.prompt: If you are an internal candidate, how can you show breadth?

options.text: Say that your manager recommended you, since their view carries weight with the panel
Say that you know the department well, since this is the main advantage an internal candidate has
Show you look beyond your current team and understand wider priorities
Say that you have worked there longest, since long service shows that you are committed

questions.hint: Breadth shows readiness.

questions.prompt: Asked what you would do if unsuccessful, which answer is best?

options.text: Say you would appeal, since that is the usual response when a candidate is sure they were the best
Say you would be disappointed and would stop applying, so that you do not waste the panel's time
Ask for feedback, work on development areas and apply again when ready
Say you would look for work outside the Civil Service, since another employer may value your skills more

questions.hint: Resilience is valued.

questions.prompt: What is a sound way to handle any challenging question?

options.text: Pause briefly, use a clear structure and be honest
Deflect the question with a joke, so that the atmosphere stays relaxed
Give a general answer, so that you do not commit yourself to a view that the panel could challenge
Answer immediately, so that you show confidence and keep the interview moving

questions.hint: Calm structure helps.

questions.prompt: A panellist asks about your health. What should you do?

options.text: Answer in detail, so that you do not seem uncooperative and the panel can understand any limits
Ask them why they need to know, so that the panel is made aware that the question is unfair
Leave the interview, since a panel that asks this question is not acting fairly
Steer politely back to the role's requirements and report it afterwards if concerned

questions.hint: Such questions are not appropriate.

items.title: L12: Learning from patterns in feedback
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles and CIPD guidance on feedback (public)
items.body:
Feedback from one interview is useful. Feedback from several is more useful still, because patterns appear that a single set of comments hides. If three different panels have said that your answers lack a clear result, you have found a real development area, not bad luck.

Keep a simple log after each interview and each piece of feedback. Record the date, the role, the Behaviours tested, the score if given, the comments and your own reflection. Look for repeats: comments about your own role, structure, pace, results, or the level of the examples. Examples that are too junior for the grade are a common finding, and the fix is to gather evidence at the next level, not to describe the same events better.

When you receive feedback, it can help to ask: what one thing would have changed my score most? Thank the person who gives it. If you disagree, keep that to yourself in the conversation; consider later whether there is truth in it.

A model that can help structure feedback you give or receive is situation, behaviour, impact: the situation, what the person did and the effect it had. It makes feedback specific and less personal. Use it when you ask a manager or colleague for feedback on your leadership: 'In the team meeting last week, what did you notice about how I handled the discussion?'

Build development around the patterns. You might ask for a stretch assignment, shadow a senior colleague, join a cross-department network or find a mentor. A mentor who has sat on panels can be especially useful. Plan practice interviews with someone who will give honest answers and record at least one of them so that you can hear your own pace and filler words.

questions.prompt: Why is feedback from several interviews often more useful than from one?

options.text: It guarantees that a later promotion board will rate you higher, because they see your history
Panels give longer feedback to candidates who have applied several times, so more detail becomes available
Patterns appear that a single set of comments hides
Each panel gives the same score for the same answer, so repeated results confirm your level

questions.hint: Repeated comments point to a real development area.

questions.prompt: Three panels say your answers lack a clear result. What does this suggest?

options.text: Bad luck with the panels you happened to have, which is likely to change at the next interview
That the Behaviour is not relevant to the grade, so you should not prepare for it again
That your examples are too long, so the panel never reached the result
A real development area in how you describe outcomes

questions.hint: Repeated feedback is a pattern.

questions.prompt: Which details are useful in a feedback log?

options.text: The names of the panellists and their grades, so you can judge whose comments to trust most
The number of candidates at each interview, so that you can see how competitive each one was
Date, role, Behaviours tested, comments and your own reflection
The salary on offer, so that you can compare the value of each role you applied for

questions.hint: A log helps you find repeats.

questions.prompt: Feedback says your examples were too junior for the grade. What is the best response?

options.text: Describe the same events more impressively, using stronger language to show the scale of the work
Choose examples from an earlier job, because a longer history shows more breadth of experience
Gather evidence at the next level, for example through stretch work
Avoid giving examples and speak about your approach in general terms, so that the grade is not an issue

questions.hint: Evidence must match the level.

questions.prompt: What can you ask at the end of a feedback conversation?

options.text: What one thing would have changed my score most?
Can the decision be changed, if I send additional evidence in writing after the interview?
Who else applied, so that I can see how I compared with the candidates who were successful?
Why did I not get the job, since the panel can tell you the specific reason for the decision?

questions.hint: It focuses the feedback on an action.

questions.prompt: What does situation, behaviour, impact help you do?

options.text: Remove emotion from the interview, so that the panel's feedback stays factual
Make feedback specific and less personal
Compare candidates, so that each person can see where they ranked in the competition
Make feedback longer and more detailed, so that the person receiving it can follow it easily

questions.hint: It describes what happened and its effect.

questions.prompt: Which request for feedback follows that model?

options.text: In the team meeting last week, what did you notice about how I handled the discussion?
Am I a good leader, in your view, based on everything you have seen of me over the year?
Do I need to change the way I work, or is my current approach acceptable for the grade?
What do you think of me, and is there anything about my manner that you would change?

questions.hint: It asks about a specific situation.

questions.prompt: Which action best builds development around feedback patterns?

options.text: Change department, since a different environment will give you fresh opportunities
Wait for the next round of feedback, so that you can see whether the pattern repeats
Apply for as many roles as possible, so that you gain interview practice from more panels
Ask for a stretch assignment or find a mentor who has sat on panels

questions.hint: Targeted development addresses the pattern.

questions.prompt: How can you hear your own pace and filler words in practice?

options.text: Read your prepared answers aloud on your own, because they will sound the same as in the room
Record a practice interview and listen back
Time each answer with a stopwatch, because only length matters when it comes to pace
Ask the panel to give you a recording of your own interview, so that you can hear how you came across

questions.hint: A recording gives direct evidence.

questions.prompt: Why keep perspective after a rejection?

options.text: Candidates can always appeal a result, so a good performance is rarely wasted
Selection is competitive and good performance can still lose out
Feedback is rarely accurate, so you should not make changes to how you prepare
Panels rarely score fairly, so a result tells you little about your performance

questions.hint: Focus on what you can control.
